candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls (or can influence) the HTTP response of a host the application contacts with the WebClient: a 3xx status plus an attacker-chosen `Location` (compromised/malicious upstream endpoint, an open redirect on the contacted site, a hostile API the app calls, or an on-path attacker on a plain-HTTP hop). The payload (the victim host's cookie header / token) is then delivered to the attacker's host by the library itself.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Considered that copying user-set headers on redirect may be intentional: but the copy also includes the `cookie` entries that the library itself injected for the previous host, which the same class scopes by domain on the CookieStore path and documents as domain/path-scoped. Checked `CookieStoreImpl.get` (reversed-domain matching, path/secure checks) — it would NOT return host A's cookies for host B, so the leak is caused only by the header copy plus the missing reset in `prepareRedirectRequest`. Checked that `prepareRequest` is not re-invoked for redirects (FOLLOW_REDIRECT only runs `processRedirectCookies`), so the stale cookies are not cleaned. Checked `HttpRequestImpl.headers()` returns the internal map (line 192-196) and that `HttpContext` keeps the same `request` object across phases, so the copy really transports those entries. Also verified the redirect phase is reachable by default (DEFAULT_FOLLOW_REDIRECTS = true; maxRedirects default) and that `session.addHeader` credentials are placed in that same map (WebClientSessionAware.java:36-46).
candidates.impact: Disclosure of an authenticated session cookie and/or bearer token for the original origin to an arbitrary third-party origin chosen by the redirect. The receiving party can replay the cookie/token against the original site (session hijacking, account/API takeover), and additionally learns the token value in cleartext. This contradicts the documented contract that `WebClientSession` "honors the cookies attributes: domain, path, secure, max-age and expires" (WebClientSession.java:27-33) and the intent expressed in `processRedirectResponse`'s comment ("we need to send cookies only to the domains we received them from", SessionAwareInterceptor.java:91-95).
candidates.prerequisites: Application uses `WebClientSession.create(...)` (or otherwise sets Cookie/Authorization headers on the request) and leaves redirect following enabled — `WebClientOptions.DEFAULT_FOLLOW_REDIRECTS = true` (WebClientOptions.java:51) is propagated to each request in `HttpRequestImpl` (followRedirects = options.isFollowRedirects()). The contacted origin must return a 3xx whose `Location` is a different host; the cookie store must hold a cookie for the first host (any session-authenticated call) or the app must have set a credential header via `WebClientSession.addHeader` (the module's own example does exactly this: `session.addHeader("my-jwt-token", jwtToken)` in WebClientSessionExamples.java:14-17).
candidates.root_cause: `HttpContext.receiveResponse` copies the entire mutable request header map onto the redirect request (`nextRequest.headers().addAll(request.headers)`, HttpContext.java:215-218). That same map is mutated by `SessionAwareInterceptor.prepareRequest`, which clears it, re-adds the client headers and then appends the cookies retrieved for the *original* host from the cookie store (`request.headers().add("cookie", ...)`, SessionAwareInterceptor.java:53-65). On the redirect phase (`processRedirectCookies` -> `prepareRedirectRequest`) the interceptor only adds the cookies for the *new* host (SessionAwareInterceptor.java:113-124); it never removes/resets the inherited headers, even though it retrieves the stored original-header snapshot at lines 107-111 and never uses it, and even though `prepareRequest`'s own comment states headers "must be reset at every send because cookies can be changed" (lines 53-54). Result: host A's Cookie header (and any `WebClientSession.addHeader` value such as an Authorization/JWT header) is transmitted to host B whenever host A answers with a 3xx pointing at host B.
candidates.title: WebClientSession forwards the original origin's cookies (and addHeader credentials) to a different host when following a redirect
candidates.trace: 1) `WebClientSession.create(webClient)` -> `WebClientSessionAware` registers `SessionAwareInterceptor` on the interceptor chain (WebClientSessionAware.java:26-30); the chain is handed to every `HttpContext` (WebClientBase.java:286-289). 2) PREPARE_REQUEST: `SessionAwareInterceptor.prepareRequest` stores a snapshot of the current request headers under key `_originalHeaders`, clears `request.headers()`, re-adds the snapshot plus `webclient.headers()`, then appends the cookies matching the target host and path (`cookieStore().get(request.ssl, domain, request.uri)`) to that same map (SessionAwareInterceptor.java:47-65). 3) SEND_REQUEST: `HttpContext.handlePrepareRequest` builds the real `HttpClientRequest` and copies `request.headers` into it (HttpContext.java:355-357) — cookies/token go to host A, as intended. 4) Host A replies 302/303 with a `Location` for host B; `HttpContext.receiveResponse` (followRedirects default true, maxRedirects default) asks `client.redirectHandler()` for the next request and then executes `nextRequest.headers().addAll(request.headers)` (HttpContext.java:207-218), copying host A's `cookie` header (and any credential header added via `addHeader`) into the request that will be sent to host B. 5) FOLLOW_REDIRECT: `prepareRedirectRequest` computes the new domain and only *adds* the store cookies valid for host B (SessionAwareInterceptor.java:113-124); nothing removes the leaked host-A cookies, and the snapshot fetched at lines 107-111 is unused. 6) The leaked cookies/credentials therefore appear on the wire to host B.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-verified (no code executed; finding is source-level). vertx-core is not part of the snapshot, so I could not inspect `HttpClient.redirectHandler()`/`HttpClientRequestImpl` to confirm that the default handler follows absolute cross-host `Location` values and to confirm it does not itself strip Cookie/Authorization headers before `HttpContext.receiveResponse` runs; if the core handler refused cross-host redirects or stripped credentials, the leak would be limited to same-host redirects (where the duplicated cookie is harmless). I also could not diff against the upstream 3.9.x/4.x sources in this run, so I cannot exclude that this behaviour is inherited upstream rather than specific to this snapshot; the unused `_originalHeaders` lookup in `prepareRedirectRequest` (lines 107-111) is consistent with a missing reset step but is not proof.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-598/CWE-522 — disclosure of session cookie/credentials to an unintended party via cross-origin redirect

coverage_summary: Files: 338 source-root files (294 Java; also JS/HTML/XML/pom resources), all enumerated; the assigned scope excludes binaries and symlinks (0 excluded) and applies the same filters as B0. The P1 index covers 335/338 files (232 parsed, 3 missing), syntax-only, with no data-flow, control-flow, semantic resolution or reachability — it was used only for navigation and its labels were verified against source. I read in depth: vertx-web routing/dispatch (RouterImpl, RouterState, RouteImpl/RouteState matching, RoutingContextImpl/Wrapper/Base, HttpServerRequestWrapper), handlers (Session, CSRF, Cors, FormLogin/Redirect/OAuth2/JWT auth, Body, Static, Template, Error, Favicon, MultiTenant, Logger), SockJS/EventBusBridge transports, session stores (Local/Clustered/AbstractSession), vertx-web-client (HttpContext, SessionAwareInterceptor, CookieStoreImpl, WebClientOptions/Session, request/predicate/multipart internals), web-api-contract validation (BaseValidationHandler, type validators, XMLTypeValidator, OpenAPI3 path resolver/router factory, SecurityHandlersStore), graphql handlers, and the template engines. Not read in depth: large bundled web assets (vertx-web-graphql GraphiQL static JS ~840 KB, vertx-web/src/client/*.js), example/DTO/interface files, and build scripts beyond a scan. No code, tests, scanners or daemons were executed; no runtime confirmation exists for any statement.
limitations: No execution: findings are source-level only; the candidate's wire behaviour (does the redirect request really carry the copied Cookie header to another host) was not confirmed at runtime.

vertx-core (HttpUtils.normalizePath/removeDots, URIDecoder, HttpClient redirectHandler/HttpClientRequestImpl, HttpClientResponse) is not part of the snapshot, so several path/redirect questions could not be closed; StaticHandler path-traversal analysis and the exact redirect-following semantics depend on that code.

No upstream comparison was possible in this run, so I cannot distinguish an inherited upstream weakness from a snapshot-specific regression, nor confirm whether the redirect header reset existed in an earlier revision.
No test sources, fixtures or CI logs are present in the snapshot, so intended behaviour could only be inferred from comments/javadoc.
The P1 index is syntactic only (no data-flow/reachability/DI semantics); it cannot establish exploitability, and 3 source files are absent from it.
Bundled generated web assets (GraphiQL static JS, client-side vertxbus.js) were not audited line by line; they could hide additional client-side issues.
Some handler/DTO files (e.g. handler interfaces, WebExamples) were skimmed rather than fully read, so a low-signal issue in those areas cannot be excluded.

rejected_leads.lead: StaticHandlerImpl path handling (decode + removeDots + Utils.pathOffset) possibly allowing traversal outside the webroot (StaticHandlerImpl.java:131, 610-614).
rejected_leads.reason: The handler decodes first and then applies `HttpUtils.removeDots(...)` (vertx-core), and the served path is webRoot + pathOffset(...); no in-snapshot defect (missing check, wrong order, wrong variable) is visible, and the decisive normalisation logic lives in vertx-core, which is not part of the snapshot. Note that decode-then-removeDots is the defensive order, so I could not substantiate a traversal.

rejected_leads.lead: ErrorHandlerImpl writes `errorMessage`/stack trace into the HTML template without escaping (ErrorHandlerImpl.java:120-133, resources/META-INF/vertx/web/vertx-web-error.html:3), i.e. potential reflected XSS.
rejected_leads.reason: Exploitation requires an application-provided failure message that embeds attacker input (e.g. ValidationException messages that include the offending value, ValidationException.java:200-203 / EnumTypeValidator.java:31-32); the default path only uses the standard HTTP status message and the default 400/500 handlers are not mounted unless the app asks for them. App-dependent and matches upstream design.

rejected_leads.lead: Path parameters can be shadowed by query parameters because `RouteState.addPathParam` only adds a route param when the name is not already in `request.params()` (RouteState.java:1016-1023).
rejected_leads.reason: Real parameter-pollution footgun, but it appears intentional (pathParams() is kept separately and is authoritative for validation), the impact is entirely application-dependent (only apps reading `request().params()`/`getParam()` for path data are affected), and no in-snapshot contradiction with documented behaviour could be established.

rejected_leads.lead: CSRFHandlerImpl issues a stateless double-submit token not bound to the session and compares the HMAC with `String.equals` (CSRFHandlerImpl.java:99-133).
rejected_leads.reason: Matches the documented design (CSRFHandler javadoc, timeout default) and the stateless behaviour is standard double-submit; the non-constant-time comparison is theoretical (remote timing against a 256-bit HMAC) and not demonstrable from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: SockJS BaseTransport echoes the client-controlled JSESSIONID cookie segment into a `Set-Cookie` response header (BaseTransport.java:132-155).
rejected_leads.reason: Only affects the requesting client's own cookie jar and mirrors the upstream sockjs-node behaviour; no cross-user impact and no CRLF injection (header value comes from the parsed Cookie header).

rejected_leads.lead: WebEnvironment uses constants `vertxweb.environment`/`VERTXWEB_ENVIRONMENT` while its javadoc names `vertx.mode`/`VERTX_MODE` (WebEnvironment.java:23-38), affecting dev-mode features (ErrorHandler stack traces, GraphiQL default enablement, cache disabling).
rejected_leads.reason: Looks like documentation drift rather than a defect; clients cannot set server system properties/environment variables, so no attacker-controlled path or security impact in either direction could be shown.

rejected_leads.lead: Template-engine loaders read arbitrary filesystem paths (PebbleVertxLoader.java:43-52, MVELTemplateEngineImpl.java:76-80, FreeMarkerTemplateLoader.java:38-53), and MVEL templates are executable code.
rejected_leads.reason: The template name is supplied by the application (TemplateHandlerImpl derives it from the normalised request path plus a configured directory), so this is a documented untrusted-template hazard rather than a demonstrable flaw in the snapshot; no missing sanitisation step was found inside these classes.

summary: Snapshot is Eclipse Vert.x Web 3.9.3 (parent pom `vertx-web-parent` 3.9.3; modules vertx-web, vertx-web-common, vertx-web-client, template engines, api-contract, api-service, graphql). I reviewed the Java sources broadly (routing/dispatch, handlers, sessions/cookies/CSRF, SockJS bridge, static/template serving, api-contract validation + OpenAPI router, GraphQL handlers, WebClient internals) plus the P1 syntactic index scope. The single strongest evidence-backed candidate is in vertx-web-client: when a redirect is followed, the whole mutable request header map (which `SessionAwareInterceptor.prepareRequest` has just populated with the cookies of the original host, and which also carries any `WebClientSession.addHeader` values such as bearer tokens/JWTs) is copied onto the redirect request, and the redirect-phase interceptor only *adds* the new host's cookies without ever resetting the inherited ones — so a cross-origin `Location` causes the previous origin's session cookies/credentials to be sent to another host. All other suspicions I examined were either app-dependent, dependent on code outside the snapshot (vertx-core), or consistent with documented/intended behaviour; they are listed as rejected leads.
